Middle English

Etymology 1

From Old English hēo, hīe. Probably a doublet of sche; see that entry for more.

Alternative forms

  • he, hie, hi, hye, hy, hoe, ho, hue, hu, hw, ȝeo, ȝe, ȝhe, ȝoe, ȝo, ȝho, yhe, yo, yio, ge, ghe, ha, a

Pronoun

heo (accusative his, heo, genitive hire, possessive determiner hires)

  2. Third-person singular feminine nominative pronoun: she
  3. Third-person singular feminine accusative pronoun: her
  4. It; used also of inanimate objects

Old English

Alternative forms

  • hæo — Anglian
  • hiu, hia, hīo

Etymology

From Proto-West Germanic *hiju, from Proto-Germanic *hijō f (“this, this one”).

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /xe͜oː/, [he͜oː]
  • Rhymes: -e͜oː

Pronoun

hēo f (accusative hīe, genitive hire, dative hire)

  1. she
    • c. 990 CE, John 20:15, in Benjamin Thorpe, F.S.A., ed. and transl., The Anglo-Saxon Version of the Holy Gospels, London: J.G.F. and J. Rivington; and J.H. Parker, published 1842, page n241:
      Hēo wēnde þæt hit sē wyrtweard wǣre. [WARNING: may be normalized]
      She thought it was the gardener.
    • 996–997, Ælfric of Eynsham, “De Transitu Mariae Aegyptiace [St. Mary of Egypt]” (Chapter XXIIIB), in Rev. Walter W. Skeat, M.A., ed. and transl., Aelfric's Lives of Saints (Early English Text Society original series 94), volume II, London: N. Trübner & Co., published 1890, page 40:
      Þā hēo þis ġehīerde, þā smearcode hēo wiþ his weardes. [WARNING: may be normalized]
      When she heard this, she smiled in his direction.
  2. it (when the thing being referred to is grammatically feminine)
    • early 8th century, Beowulf, line 455
      Gǣþ ā wyrd swā hēo sċeal.
      Fate goes always as it must.
    • c. 989–992 CE, Ælfric of Eynsham, “St. Benedict, Abbot”, in Benjamin Thorpe, F.S.A., ed. and transl., The Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church, volume II, London: Richard and John E. Taylor, published 1846, page 156:
      Sē Dēofol wearp ānne stān tō þǣre bellan þæt hēo eall tōsprang. [WARNING: may be normalized]
      The Devil threw a rock at the bell so it broke into pieces.
    • The Dialogues of Solomon and Saturn
      Sēo sunne biþ swā rēad on ǣfen for þon þe hēo lōcaþ ufan on helle.
      The sun is so red in the evening because it looks down on hell.
